title: Employee Free Time
statement:
`schedule` holds the working hours of several employees: `schedule[i]` lists the intervals during which employee `i` is at work. Each employee's intervals are sorted by start and do not overlap. Return every stretch of time that is free for **all** employees, as a list of intervals sorted by start.

- Report each free stretch whole: it starts where some work ends and runs until the next moment anyone starts working.
- Only finite stretches count, so the time before the earliest start and after the latest end is not reported.
- A free stretch must have positive length: where one interval ends exactly when another begins (for example `[1, 3]` and `[3, 5]`), there is no free time.
- If there is no free time, return an empty list.

Every interval is an `Interval` object with number fields `start` and `end`, as on LeetCode; it is not an array, so `schedule[0][0].start` works but `schedule[0][0][0]` does not. Return a list of `Interval` objects, made with `new Interval(start, end)`. Cases write each interval as a pair `[start, end]`: the judge builds the `Interval` objects before calling `employeeFreeTime` and turns your answer back into pairs. (The TypeScript starter types the values as `any` only because the signature format has no `Interval` type.)
constraints: Each employee's intervals are sorted by start and do not overlap
notes:
## Intuition

Who is working does not matter, only whether *anyone* is. So pour every employee's intervals into one list and treat it as a single busy calendar. Free time is then exactly the gaps between the merged busy blocks. Sorting by start lets one sweep do the merging: keep the latest `end` reached so far, and any interval that starts after it leaves a gap. A brute force could cut the timeline at every endpoint and test each piece against every interval, which is O(N²).

## Approach

1. Copy every employee's intervals into `intervals`.
2. Sort `intervals` by `start`.
3. Set `end` to the first interval's end: the busy block so far reaches there.
4. For each `interval` in order: if it starts after `end`, the stretch from `end` to `interval.start` is free for everyone, so add `new Interval(end, interval.start)` to `free`.
5. Extend `end` to `Math.max(end, interval.end)`, since an interval inside the block must not shrink it.
6. Return `free`; it is already sorted because the sweep moves left to right.

## Example 1, step by step

The pooled intervals sorted by start are `[1,2]`, `[1,3]`, `[4,10]`, `[5,6]`. `end` starts at 2.

- `[1,2]`: 1 is not after 2; `end` stays 2.
- `[1,3]`: 1 is not after 2; `end` becomes 3.
- `[4,10]`: 4 is after 3, so `[3,4]` is free; `end` becomes 10.
- `[5,6]`: 5 is not after 10; `end` stays 10.

The answer is `[[3,4]]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(N log N) for N intervals in total, dominated by the sort.
- Space: O(N) for the pooled list. A min-heap holding one interval per employee would merge the already sorted lists in O(N log k) for k employees.

## Pitfalls

- Use `>`, not `>=`, when testing for a gap: touching intervals leave a zero-length gap that must not be reported.
- Take the maximum when updating `end`; an interval nested inside the current block would otherwise pull it back and invent free time.
- Return `Interval` objects, not `[start, end]` arrays, and read fields with `.start` and `.end`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `intervals` | every employee's intervals in one list, sorted by start |
| `interval` | the interval being swept |
| `end` | the furthest end of the busy block built so far |
| `free` | the free intervals found, in order |
